what_its_for: Pyrazinamide is an antibiotic used to treat tuberculosis (TB), a serious infection that mainly affects the lungs. It is almost always used together with other TB medicines as part of a combination treatment plan. It works by killing or stopping the growth of the bacteria that cause TB.
how_to_take: Take pyrazinamide by mouth, exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help if it upsets your stomach. Always take all of your TB medicines together at the same time each day unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Never skip doses or stop taking this medicine early, even if you feel better, because this can make the bacteria harder to treat.
dosing: Your dose will be decided by your doctor based on your weight and how well your kidneys work. The usual adult dose is between 1,000 mg and 2,000 mg taken once daily, or it may be split into smaller doses taken throughout the day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are not sure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store pyrazinamide at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from light, heat, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking pyrazinamide, as this increases the risk of liver damage. Avoid taking medicines that contain acetaminophen (Tylenol) or other drugs that can harm your liver without first asking your doctor. Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you are taking. Avoid prolonged sun exposure, as pyrazinamide can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight — use sunscreen and wear protective clothing when outdoors.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice), dark urine or pale-colored stools, severe stomach pain, nausea or vomiting that will not stop, joint pain or swelling, a skin rash or itching, pain or burning when you urinate, unusual bleeding or bruising, fever that does not go away, or loss of appetite. These could be signs of serious side effects such as liver problems or high uric acid levels (gout).
when_it_works: Pyrazinamide starts working right away, but you may not feel better for several weeks. It is important to continue taking all of your TB medicines for the full length of treatment, which is usually 6 to 9 months or longer. Do not stop taking it just because you feel better. Your doctor will do regular blood tests and check-ups to make sure the treatment is working and that the medicine is not causing any harm.
special_populations: Kidney or liver problems: Your dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney or liver disease. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Older adults: You may be more sensitive to side effects, especially liver problems. Regular monitoring is important. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Children: Pyrazinamide can be used in children for TB treatment, but the dose is based on the child's weight and must be determined by a doctor. Gout: Tell your doctor if you have a history of gout, as this medicine can raise uric acid levels and trigger a gout attack. Diabetes: This medicine may make blood sugar harder to control. Monitor your blood sugar carefully and talk to your doctor.
